The full-support manuscript proves that an admissible integrable minimizer
of the zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has Stieltjes support equal to every overlap
scale in [0,1). The proof turns a hypothetical support gap into a constant
interval for the order parameter. Variational contact at the ends of that
interval conflicts with a strict curvature inequality inside it. Along the
auxiliary diffusion, the spatial gradient of the value function is a bounded
martingale. Full support makes this martingale's second moment equal to time;
its terminal correlation with Brownian motion gives the ground-state value.
The manuscript's further argument gives a smooth Stieltjes density, strictly
positive on $(0,1)$, and no atom at zero. Sections 9.1–9.2 derive this stronger
ordinary conclusion separately from the selected formal support statement.

This record reconstructs those arguments and follows the finite Gaussian
approximation into the separate QAOA manuscript. The latter claims that
finite deterministic circuits approach the SK optimum when system size tends
to infinity before circuit depth increases. Its circuit construction needs
additional approximation, synthesis, seed-removal and transfer arguments.
The two formal statements concern full support and scalar value
consequences; neither states QAOA circuit convergence. Their verification
scope is described at the end. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main] and
[OpenAI (2026b), Theorem 1.1][q-intro].

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, put

$$
H_n(\sigma)=\frac1{\sqrt n}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,\qquad
\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n,\qquad
P_*=\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$

For overlap $R_{12}=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i^1\sigma_i^2$, the covariance is
$nR_{12}^2/2-1/2$. Thus the convention is $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, with
$\xi''=1$. A centered Gaussian of variance $1/2$, common to all
configurations, removes the final constant without changing the expected
maximum. Every normalization below uses this convention.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous
functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ with
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Their Stieltjes measures satisfy
$\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t)$, including
$\mu_\gamma(\{0\})=\gamma(0)$. They are locally finite, but need not be
probability measures or have finite total mass. Support is relative to [0,1).

Let $B$ be standard Brownian motion. The control value and Parisi
functional are

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_{|\alpha|\le1}\mathbb E\left[
 \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right|
 -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds\right],
$$
$$
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$

Controls are progressively measurable for Brownian increments after $t$.
For a general admissible coefficient, the solution and its spatial derivatives
are locally absolutely continuous in time on compact strips; the time equation
holds almost everywhere. The control formula fixes the solution. The PDE is
$\Phi_t=-\tfrac12(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma\Phi_x^2)$, with
$\Phi(1,x)=|x|$. Auffinger and Chen's zero-temperature Parisi formula and
attainment identify $P_*$ with $\min_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$.
The support theorem itself assumes a minimizer and proves a property of it;
it does not separately supply one. See [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]
and [Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1 and proof of Lemma 3][ac2017].

Write $u=\Phi_x$, $a=\Phi_{xx}$, and
$dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$, $X_0=0$.
Write $q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]$ for the second moment of this
gradient along $X$.
The first result assumes an admissible minimizer. It constructs its
Stieltjes measure and an associated diffusion, proves
$\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma=[0,1)$ and strict increase of $\gamma$,
and obtains $\mathbb E u(t,X_t)^2=t$ and
$\mathbb E a(t,X_t)^2=1$ for every associated diffusion. The selected
formal statement has exactly this conditional scope; it does not assert a
smooth density.
Its [Lean implementation at the fixed source revision][support-main] implements the
[separately stated formal challenge][support-type]. The
[Comparator configuration][support-config] identifies the intended
comparison; the evidence retained with this draft does not establish
a successful research-target replay.

The second result concerns the scalar value. A bounded martingale ends
at a spin-valued random variable whose Brownian correlation represents
$P_*$. Finite Gaussian coefficients approximate that correlation at each
fixed $T<1$, followed by $T\uparrow1$. Its formal statement is separate
and retains the minimizer and diffusion hypotheses where needed. The QAOA
theorem goes further: for each requested accuracy it selects one finite
deterministic circuit, independent of size and disorder, whose limiting
expected energy approaches $P_*$. Neither formal statement asserts that
circuit conclusion.
The scalar clauses are in a [separate Lean implementation][value-main], with their
own [formal challenge][value-type] and [Comparator configuration][value-config].
Those links identify the selected statements, not a completed replay
receipt for either research target.

### 2.1 Structure of the argument The proof begins with regularity on strips bounded away from terminal time. It makes the diffusion $X$ and the gradient moment $q$ available, so a first variation can show where the minimizer is in contact. On a constant interval, the shape inequalities and the rational certificate give the strict curvature needed to contradict that contact. The zero-interval case uses a separate heat argument, and the possible terminal plateau needs its own exclusion. These steps lead to full support and the two moment equalities. In this manuscript route, the value argument then uses bounded-martingale convergence and the attained Parisi formula to express $P_*$ as a terminal Brownian correlation and an integral of expected curvature. Section 6 defines the terminal martingale variable and proves these equalities. The fixed-$T$ Gaussian approximation recovers this integral through Euler coupling, orthogonal normalization and mean-preserving rounding. The QAOA theorem additionally requires rooted energy identification, classical synthesis, removal of temporary seeds and transfer to fixed angles. The main route is §§3–5, then §§6–7, then §§8.1–8.6; §12 compares the two formal interfaces. The original analytic details are in [OpenAI (2026a), §§2–7][fs-main], and the circuit construction is in [OpenAI (2026b), §§2–6][q-intro]. The density theorem in §§9.1–9.2 is a further consequence of support and the PDE, not a premise of the scalar or circuit construction. The positive-temperature route in §11.1 independently supplies the same bounded classical input used for synthesis. The probability consequence in §11.2 requires a separate fixed-word second-moment theorem. These branches explain why the two selected formal statements are not a formal proof of the complete circuit theorem. These destinations separate premises of the support proof from its consequences. They locate the detailed arguments behind the short paper's support and density theorem. **The diffusion and moment identity.** For any admissible $\gamma$, the compact-strip estimates justify defining $X,q$ and computing $q'=\mathbb E a^2$; see [§2.4](#strip-estimates) and [§3.1](#gradient-moment). **Variational contact.** Minimality, admissible mass addition and compact mass removal give $G\ge0$, its vanishing on support and the contact slopes. The steps are in [§3.2](#feasible-variation), [§3.3](#measure-contact) and [§3.4](#contact-slopes). **Strict curvature.** Admissibility and a positive constant $c$ on an interval suffice; minimality is not needed. The shape comparisons, algebra and limiting argument are in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons), [§4.4](#curvature-algebra) and [§4.5](#plateau-limit). **Exclusion of gaps.** Combine contact with the appropriate positive, zero or terminal argument. The cases have separate destinations: [terminal](#terminal-gap), [bounded](#bounded-gaps) and [initial](#initial-gaps) gaps. **Positive density.** Full support comes first. Differentiated moments then give [smoothness in §9.1](#smooth-density-consequence), and a local comparison gives [strict positivity in §9.2](#positive-density). **Value and circuits.** Retain the same minimizer and diffusion through [the value identity in §6](#scalar-value-identities) and [the finite Gaussian construction in §7](#finite-gaussian-approximation). [The circuit argument in §8](#qaoa-construction) requires additional theorems. ### 2.2 The regularity available before the proof starts **Proposition 2.1 (compact-strip regularity).** For $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ and $0\le T<1$, the value has bounded, jointly continuous spatial derivatives of every positive finite order on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R$. If admissible coefficients converge in $L^1$ and their smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz terminal values converge uniformly to $|x|$, these spatial derivatives converge uniformly on each such strip. The bounds depend on the derivative order, the fixed strip and a common coefficient mass bound. Time derivatives need only exist almost everywhere across coefficient jumps. On an open constant interval, the heat formula supplies the additional time smoothness used in §4. The terminal estimate is $$ |x|\le\Phi_\gamma(t,x) \le |x|+\sqrt{2(1-t)/\pi}+\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\,ds. $$ It controls approach to $|x|$ without differentiating that cusp. The strip estimates justify the interior calculations and finite meshes; the terminal bound and integrability justify the later endpoint limits. The two roles must remain separate. Their uses depend on the region and limit. On a fixed $[0,T]$ with $T<1$, bounded spatial derivatives and locally absolutely continuous time dependence justify the Itô identities and Euler coupling. Across a jump of $\gamma$, the spatial derivative moments remain continuous and the time equations hold almost everywhere; this is enough for contact slopes and the endpoint chord comparison. Inside a constant interval, classical time differentiation permits the strict-curvature calculation. As $T\uparrow1$, the controls change: the displayed value bound, integrable coefficient tails and martingale convergence justify first variation and terminal value. No differentiated estimate at the terminal cusp is used. These are [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1 and its diffusion consequences][fs-reg]; [§2.4](#strip-estimates) reconstructs their uniformity. The hypotheses also have distinct uses. Zero field supplies evenness, $u(0,0)=0$ and reflection in the shape argument. The convention $\xi''=1$ fixes the curvature coefficients. Monotonicity gives bounded coefficients before time one and nonnegative coefficient jumps; it also turns a support gap into a constant interval. Integrability controls terminal tails and Fubini interchanges, while local finiteness of the Stieltjes measure is enough for compact mass removal. Minimality first enters through the variational inequality in §3; the constant-interval curvature estimate itself applies to an admissible coefficient without assuming it is a minimiser. [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]; [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [OpenAI (2026a), §6][fs-var]. ### 2.3 Which prior results play which role The imported ground-state formula supplies two facts with different uses. Auffinger and Chen's Theorem 1 identifies the ground-state limit with an infimum over $\mathcal U$. To choose a coefficient attaining that infimum, one must also use their construction in the proof of Lemma 3. In the cited arXiv v2, the theorem is on p. 3, the compactness construction is on pp. 7–9, and the lower-bound proof is on pp. 11–12. The support proof is conditional on a minimizer. From that hypothesis, continue directly with [the compact-strip estimates in §2.4](#strip-estimates). The construction below explains how attainment supplies the minimizer later used in the value and circuit arguments. Here is the part of that construction which supplies the witness. Let $\alpha_\beta$ be a positive-temperature Parisi distribution function. The source bounds $\beta\alpha_\beta(t)$ uniformly on each interval ending before one. Helly selection and a diagonal subsequence produce a nonnegative, nondecreasing right-continuous limit $\gamma_0$. In the SK normalization, the source's weighted integral bound also controls $\int_0^1\beta\alpha_\beta(t)\,dt$. For every nonnegative nondecreasing $h$, splitting at $1/2$ gives $\int_0^1 h(t)\,dt\le4\int_0^1t h(t)\,dt$: the first half is bounded by $h(1/2)/2$, and on the second half $t\ge1/2$. Fatou's lemma then gives $\gamma_0\in\mathcal U$. Mass can concentrate at time one during this limit, so compact convergence alone does not identify the limiting control problem. Write the limiting measure of the time coefficients as $$ \nu_0(dt)=\gamma_0(t)\,dt+m\delta_1(dt),\qquad m\geq0. $$ For an arbitrary admissible control, let $S$ denote its terminal state with coefficient $\gamma_0$. To see why the terminal choice is admissible, let the original control be $\alpha$ and put $S_s=B_s+\int_0^s\gamma_0(r)\alpha_r\,dr$. For a cutoff $\tau<1$ use $\alpha_s$ before $\tau$ and $g_k(S_s)$ afterwards, where $g_k$ is a continuous function bounded by one and converging pointwise to the sign with $\operatorname{sgn}(0)=1$. This control uses only information available at time $s$. At fixed $\tau,k$, first take the temperature limit; then let $\tau\uparrow1$ and $k\to\infty$. The continuous terminal evaluation has thereby approached $\operatorname{sgn}(S)$ without anticipating a future state. The endpoint atom then contributes $$ |S+m\operatorname{sgn}(S)|-|S|=m $$ to the reward and $$ \tfrac12m\bigl(\operatorname{sgn}(S)^2+1\bigr)=m $$ to the combined control and Parisi penalties. These contributions cancel. Taking the supremum over the remaining controls proves $P_*\geq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)$. The upper bound proved earlier in that paper gives $P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma)$. Therefore $$ P_*\leq\inf_{\gamma\in\mathcal U}\mathcal P(\gamma) \leq\mathcal P(\gamma_0)\leq P_*. $$ Thus $\gamma_0$ attains the infimum. The cancellation is a step in the imported existence proof; it is not an additional assumption about the Stieltjes measure $d\gamma_0$. In particular, $\nu_0$ here is the limit of coefficient-times-Lebesgue measures, not the order parameter's Stieltjes measure. The two measures must not be identified. [Auffinger and Chen, arXiv:1606.05335v2, pp. 7–12][ac17]. The cited theorem is stated for the almost-sure normalized maximum. Its expected-value formulation used here follows from Gaussian concentration. For $L_n=n^{-1}\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma)$, the Lipschitz constant in the Gaussian couplings is $\sqrt{(n-1)/(2n^2)}$. Hence $L_n-\mathbb E L_n\to0$ in probability. Since the almost-sure limit is the deterministic Parisi value, the deterministic sequence $\mathbb E L_n$ has the same limit. The full-support theorem below remains conditional on a minimizer; neither of the selected formal interfaces constructs one. [OpenAI full-support manuscript, Introduction, ground-state formula and its footnote][fs-main]. Auffinger–Chen–Zeng's infinite support does not exclude an interior gap. Their terminal-plateau observation anticipates one endpoint obstruction; the argument below supplies the quantitative boundary-layer proof used here. The full-support manuscript develops a rational coercivity route and credits Chen's 2026 theorem for the same full-support conclusion and smooth absolute continuity. Chen's Proposition 4.2 has the conditional crossing form $q''(t)=0\Rightarrow q'''(t)>0$; the cited rational certificate gives $q'''(t)>0$ throughout a positive constant interval. These are different sufficient mechanisms, and this record makes no priority claim for full support. [Auffinger, Chen and Zeng (2020), Theorem 1 and Remark 7][acz]; [Chen (2026), Theorem 1.3 and Proposition 4.2][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The transformed density comparisons also have antecedents in Lopatto's positive-temperature analysis and Chen's zero-temperature analysis; the rational coercive identity is the different step in the full-support proof. Zhou's positive-temperature interval-support result applies near the critical temperature, whereas Lopatto's cited theorem covers the low-temperature zero-field phase. Neither transfers full Stieltjes support to zero temperature on its own: for the minimizers, $\beta\mu_\beta$ converges vaguely on $[0,1)$ to the zero-temperature Stieltjes measure, while the unscaled Parisi probability measures converge weakly on $[0,1]$ to $\delta_1$. These are different measures and topologies. Convergence without an interval-specific lower bound can lose support information. The direct zero-temperature gap proof below is therefore essential. [Chen (2026), Remarks 1.4–1.5][chen2026]; [OpenAI (2026a), §§1–2][fs-main]. The coefficient classes in this comparison can be translated explicitly. In the positive-temperature convention, write $$ U_t=-\frac{\beta^2}{2}(U_{yy}+\alpha_\nu U_y^2), \qquad U(1,y)=\log\cosh y. $$ Set $\Phi_\beta(t,x)=\beta^{-1}U(t,\beta x)$ and $\gamma_\beta=\beta\alpha_\nu$. Direct differentiation gives $$ (\Phi_\beta)_t=-\tfrac12\bigl((\Phi_\beta)_{xx} +\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x^2\bigr),\qquad \Phi_\beta(1,x)=\beta^{-1}\log\cosh(\beta x). $$ Dividing the associated diffusion by $\beta$ likewise gives unit Brownian noise and drift $\gamma_\beta(\Phi_\beta)_x$. Conversely, every bounded nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous coefficient on $[0,1)$ has this form: choose $\beta>0$ at least its supremum, take distribution function $\alpha_\nu=\gamma/\beta$ below one, and put the remaining probability mass at one. This identifies coefficient classes, not minimizers at different temperatures. The terminal values differ from $|x|$ by at most $(\log2)/\beta$, but passing a strict inequality to the cusp and to coefficients unbounded near one still needs uniform estimates. A qualitative crossing statement alone supplies no positive limiting fourth-moment margin. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, equation (1.2), §2 and Proposition 5.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4). Two related works sharpen the comparison without entering the pinned September proof. [Lopatto, arXiv:2607.11756v4, Proposition 5.1 and (5.8)–Corollary 5.6](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.11756v4), proves a conditional curvature crossing on a positive constant interval. Its integrating factor makes a transformed curvature derivative strictly increasing, so the associated contact derivative decreases and then increases; it does not assert an unconditional positive third derivative. [Lopatto, arXiv:2610.00127v1, Theorem 2.3 and §8](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.00127v1), works at positive temperature and positive external field. Its comparison requires one-sided bounds on the coefficient before and after the chosen time, a moment inequality and a stationarity equality. Several of these conditions are automatic in its density application: monotonicity supplies the one-sided bounds at a continuity point, contact on a full-support interval makes the scalar inequality an equality, and the quotient formula for the coefficient supplies stationarity. Its moment bootstrap then gives smooth, strictly positive density on a nontrivial support interval; a singleton support is a separate case. Appendix B, Theorem B.1 and equation (B.1), also prove strict positivity in the zero-field positive-temperature setting, where the extra noncentered-law condition is unnecessary. These results are therefore close analytic antecedents. The distinction used below is the unconditional quantitative fourth-moment margin for the comparison coefficient and its controlled passage to the zero-temperature cusp. Here is an explicit example of the information lost in such a limit. It concerns admissible measures, not Parisi minimizers. Put $g=\mathbf1_{[0,1/3]\cup[2/3,1)}$ and $q_n=1-n^{-2}$, and for $n\ge2$ define $$ \mu_n(dt)=\frac{g(t)+n^{-1}}n\mathbf1_{[0,q_n]}(t)\,dt +\left(1-\frac1n\int_0^{q_n}(g(t)+n^{-1})\,dt\right)\delta_{q_n}(dt). $$ The continuous part has mass at most $(2/3+1/n)/n<1$, so these are probability measures with a positive endpoint atom. Their density is positive throughout $[0,q_n]$, giving $\operatorname{supp}\mu_n=[0,q_n]$. Their continuous mass tends to zero and $q_n\to1$, hence $\mu_n\Rightarrow\delta_1$ weakly on $[0,1]$. For a compactly supported continuous test function on $[0,1)$, the endpoint atom eventually lies outside its support. Consequently $n\mu_n\to g(t)\,dt$ vaguely there, although the limit vanishes on $(1/3,2/3)$. Even the cumulative coefficients converge in the topology used for the PDE: with $\gamma_n(t)=n\mu_n([0,t])$ and $\gamma(t)=\int_0^t g(s)\,ds$, their difference is $t/n$ below $q_n$, and $\gamma_n=n$ on the terminal strip of length $n^{-2}$. Thus $$ \|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}\le\frac1{2n}+\frac1n\longrightarrow0. $$ Every $\gamma_n$ is admissible, but $d\gamma$ has an interior gap. Minimality and the gap argument supply information that these convergences alone do not. An atom added at time one is likewise invisible to the coefficient on $[0,1)$ and hence to its PDE and variational functional; the zero-temperature problem does not select an endpoint mass. Control and gradient-martingale methods have antecedents in [Auffinger–Chen](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00220-014-2254-z) and [Jagannath–Tobasco](https://arxiv.org/abs/1502.04398v4). A finite-temperature theorem with smooth terminal value $\log\cosh$ does not alone establish the result with terminal cusp $|x|$. The required compact-strip and terminal estimates are supplied in [OpenAI (2026a), §2][fs-reg]; [Chen–Handschy–Lerman](https://arxiv.org/abs/1609.04368v4) supplies earlier zero-temperature regularity, control and uniqueness results (Theorem 4 for uniqueness). This is distinct from the earlier finite-temperature uniqueness result of Auffinger and Chen. [Montanari](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.10897v2) and [El Alaoui–Montanari–Sellke](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00904v1) inform normalised discretisation and optimisation. The particular shifted Gaussian coefficient identity used here is proved in [OpenAI (2026a), §7][fs-cons].

The curvature argument needs estimates uniform over the approximating
coefficients. Here is the route from the control formula to those estimates;
all bounds are taken on a fixed strip ending before time one.

For finite-step coefficients and a smooth, even, convex, one-Lipschitz
terminal function $\psi$, the evolution through a step of height $c$ is
$$
\Phi(t,x)=
\begin{cases}
c^{-1}\log P_{b-t}(e^{c\Phi(b,\cdot)})(x),&c>0,\\
P_{b-t}\Phi(b,\cdot)(x),&c=0,
\end{cases}
$$
where $P_h$ denotes convolution with a centred Gaussian of variance $h$.
The heat formula preserves evenness, convexity and the spatial Lipschitz
bound. Along a controlled path $dY_s=\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds+dB_s$, the drift
of the value minus the accumulated control cost is
$-\gamma(s)(\alpha_s-\Phi_x(s,Y_s))^2/2$. It is nonpositive, and is zero
for the feedback control. This proves the stated control formula for the
smooth step problem, including attainability by its feedback diffusion.

Using the same control in two such problems and then taking suprema gives
$$
\|\Phi_{\gamma,\psi}-\Phi_{\widetilde\gamma,\widetilde\psi}\|_\infty
\le \|\psi-\widetilde\psi\|_\infty
       +\frac32\|\gamma-\widetilde\gamma\|_{L^1(0,1)}.
$$
The drift part costs at most the coefficient difference in $L^1$, by the
terminal Lipschitz bound; the quadratic cost contributes another half of
that difference. The supremum norm is of the difference of the values,
which is bounded even though each value grows linearly in $x$.
With $\psi_M(x)=M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$,
$0\le\psi_M-|x|\le(\log2)/M$. Choose simultaneously $\gamma_m\to\gamma$ in $L^1$ and $M_m\to\infty$.
These are two distinct requirements: $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ alone
does not force terminal convergence. This compatible approximation
determines a unique uniform limiting value. Its terminal bound,
given in §2.2, also follows directly: choose the zero control for the lower
bound, and use $|\alpha|-\alpha^2/2\le1/2$ for the upper bound.

To obtain spatial derivatives, choose $T<b<1$. Monotonicity gives the
uniform coefficient estimate
$$
\gamma(t)\le\frac{\|\gamma\|_1}{1-b}\quad(0\le t\le b).
$$
An $L^1$-convergent family thus has a common coefficient bound $\Gamma$ on
this larger strip. For its smooth step approximants, put $U=\Phi_x$.
The differentiated mild equation is
$$
U(t)=P_{b-t}U(b)+\int_t^b\gamma(s)P_{s-t}[U(s)U_x(s)]\,ds.
$$
Since $\|U\|_\infty\le1$ and
$\|\partial_xP_hF\|_\infty\le Ch^{-1/2}\|F\|_\infty$,
$$
\|U_x(t)\|_\infty\le\frac C{\sqrt{b-t}}
 +C\Gamma\int_t^b\frac{\|U_x(s)\|_\infty}{\sqrt{s-t}}\,ds.
$$
Substituting this inequality once into its own integral uses
$\int_t^s((r-t)(s-r))^{-1/2}\,dr=\pi$. It reduces the estimate to an
ordinary backward Gronwall inequality with integrable forcing. This bounds
$U_x$ uniformly on $[0,T]$ without any terminal derivative bound. Repeating
on successively smaller strips bounds each higher spatial derivative: put
one derivative on the heat kernel and the rest on $UU_x$; only the term
$U\partial_x^mU$ contains the new highest derivative. The remaining products
have already been bounded.

Uniform convergence of the values then yields convergence of every
positive spatial derivative. For a bounded twice differentiable difference
$F$ with bounded second derivative, Taylor's formula gives
$$
\|F'\|_\infty\le \frac{2\|F\|_\infty}{h}
                         +\frac h2\|F''\|_\infty\qquad(h>0).
$$
First choose $h$ small using the common second-derivative bound, then make
$\|F\|_\infty$ small. Iterate on derivative differences. Passing to the
integral form of the differentiated PDE proves local absolute continuity
in time and its almost-everywhere equations. No classical time derivative
at a coefficient jump, and no derivative of $|x|$ at its cusp, is being
assumed.

Finally, couple all feedback diffusions with the same Brownian motion.
On $[0,T]$, let $L$ be a common spatial Lipschitz bound for their drifts.
The difference of the two integral equations gives, for example,
$$
\sup_{s\le T}|X_s^n-X_s|
\le e^{LT}\left(\|\gamma_n-\gamma\|_1
 +\|\gamma_n\|_1\|u_n-u\|_{\infty,[0,T]\times\mathbb R}\right)
 \longrightarrow0.
$$
This is a deterministic bound under the coupling. The derivative bounds
one order higher ensure uniform continuity when derivatives are evaluated
at these moving points. Every fixed polynomial in the bounded derivatives
therefore converges in expectation. This is precisely the convergence
needed for the integrated curvature expression in §4; none of the forward
density scores or their quotients need converge.

### 2.5 Order of approximation

The same symbol for a small error must not conceal changing background
objects. The following account fixes those objects before the indicated
limit. A single admissible minimiser and its associated diffusion are
retained throughout the scalar construction.

**Compact-strip regularity.** Fix a derivative order $k\ge1$, a cutoff
$T<1$ and a common coefficient $L^1$ bound. Coefficients converge in $L^1$
within that bound; spatial derivatives converge uniformly on the strip.

**Shape inequalities on a plateau.** Fix the height $c>0$ and a closed
interior neighbourhood. Choose step coefficients equal to $c$ there and
smooth terminal values with $M_m\ge\|\gamma_m\|_\infty$ and
$M_m\to\infty$. The coefficient and terminal approximations may be
chosen as one compatible sequence.

**First variation.** Fix $\gamma$, a feasible $\eta\in L^1$ and initially
$\epsilon>0$. Remove the terminal cutoff before letting
$\epsilon\downarrow0$. The terminal remainder divided by $\epsilon$ is
bounded by an $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

**Terminal value.** Keep the chosen minimiser and diffusion fixed. Bounded
martingale convergence and integrability of $\gamma$ justify
$t\uparrow1$; no terminal derivative bound is needed.

**Finite Gaussian coefficients.** Fix $\gamma,X$ and $T<1$. Refine $N$
using the fixed-strip bounds, then control the remaining value tail by $1-T$.

For the plateau transfer, tail estimates for a fixed approximant may depend
on that approximant. The passage to the limit uses the integrated
polynomial in the scaled second, third and fourth spatial derivatives of
the value function and the common strip bounds; it does not require
uniform bounds on the auxiliary density scores. Sections 3 and 4 explain
the variation and plateau-transfer arguments, and §7 gives a complete scalar error
budget. The further choices used to produce a circuit appear in §8.6.
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1, Lemma 6.1, Proposition 5.1 and
Proposition 7.2][fs-main].

**Proposition 3.1 (variational contact).** For an admissible minimizer, the potential $G(s)=\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt$ is nonnegative on $[0,1)$ and vanishes on $S=\operatorname{supp}\mu_\gamma$. At every $s\in S$, $q(s)=s$ and $q'(s)\le1$, with a right derivative at zero. The minimisation takes place over nonnegative Stieltjes measures with an integrable cumulative function. **Abstract.** The Stieltjes measure of every integrable minimiser of the
zero-temperature Parisi functional for the pure, zero-field
Sherrington–Kirkpatrick model has full support on $[0,1)$ and a smooth
density that is strictly positive on $(0,1)$. We reconstruct OpenAI's quantitative
argument, organised around two uses of one spatial-moment inequality.
On a positive constant interval, it makes the derivative of the gradient
second moment strictly convex, contradicting the endpoint conditions
imposed by minimality. The same curvature and the bounded gradient
also exclude terminal gaps. Full support then gives moment identities and
smoothness; a local constant replacement transfers the inequality to the minimiser and
forces its density to be positive. H.-B. Chen previously proved full support
and smooth nonnegative density. We isolate the fixed-time spatial moment
and the positive margin that survives local replacement, while importing its
shape comparisons and full polynomial identity. We also derive the scalar value
identity and explain its classical optimisation consequence. For the quantum approximate
optimization algorithm (QAOA), we identify the rooted energy of a finite Gaussian
observable and the separate circuit theorem that approximates it. A further
second-moment theorem gives a measured near-optimal configuration on the same
random instance, with the circuit word fixed before the number of spins grows.

For independent standard Gaussian couplings $J_{ij}$, the pure,
zero-field [Sherrington–Kirkpatrick (SK) Hamiltonian][SK] is
$$
H_n(\sigma)=n^{-1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}\sigma_i\sigma_j,
\qquad \sigma\in\{-1,1\}^n.
$$
The limiting ground-state energy per spin, with the maximisation
convention, is
$$
P_*:=\lim_{n\to\infty}n^{-1}\mathbb E\max_\sigma H_n(\sigma).
$$
The Parisi formula expresses $P_*$ as a minimum over nondecreasing
functions. Our subject is the structure of a minimiser: its increments
charge every interval of overlap scales below one, and in fact have
strictly positive density at each interior scale. The proof uses one
quantitative bound twice, first to exclude constant intervals and then,
after an approximation, to prove pointwise positivity.

For two configurations, their overlap is
$R(\sigma,\tau)=n^{-1}\sum_i\sigma_i\tau_i$. It determines the
energy covariance: $\mathbb E[H_n(\sigma)H_n(\tau)]=nR^2/2-1/2$.
Thus the Gaussian law of the energies is encoded by the overlaps.
We use the covariance convention $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, so $\xi''=1$;
adding one independent centred Gaussian of
variance $1/2$ to every configuration's energy gives covariance
$n\xi(R)$ and leaves the expected maximum unchanged. This is the
normalisation of the ground-state Parisi formula of
[Auffinger and Chen (2017), Theorem 1][AC]. There are no higher-order
interactions and no external field.

Let $\mathcal U$ consist of the nonnegative, nondecreasing,
right-continuous functions $\gamma:[0,1)\to[0,\infty)$ satisfying
$\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty$. Define the locally finite Stieltjes
measure by
$$
\mu_\gamma([0,t])=\gamma(t),\qquad 0\leq t<1.
$$
Thus $\mu_\gamma((s,t])=\gamma(t)-\gamma(s)$: the measure records
the increments of $\gamma$. A point mass (atom) of size $\gamma(0)$
is allowed at zero, and the total mass need not be finite or equal
to one. All support statements use the relative topology of $[0,1)$.
A support gap is a relatively open interval of positive length with
zero mass; the cumulative coefficient is constant on such an interval.

The Parisi functional $\mathcal P(\gamma)$ is defined using an
auxiliary value function $\Phi_\gamma(t,x)$, where $x\in\mathbb R$
is a spatial variable and $t$ is the overlap parameter, treated as
time in the equation. Write $\Phi=\Phi_\gamma$ and use subscripts
for partial derivatives. The backward equation, terminal condition
and functional are
$$
\Phi_t=-\tfrac12\bigl(\Phi_{xx}+\gamma(t)\Phi_x^2\bigr),
\qquad \Phi(1,x)=|x|,
\qquad
\mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0)-\tfrac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt.
$$
The terminal value $|x|$ is the zero-temperature value of one spin
in a field $x$. For an integrable
coefficient, the PDE solution is interpreted by approximation from
bounded monotone coefficients. The exact control
definition and stability theorem are [OpenAI (2026a), §1 and
Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS]. To turn minimality of $\mathcal P$ into a
condition on $\gamma$, we use a random process whose gradient moment
measures the first-order cost of changing $\gamma$. Write $u=\Phi_x$ for the spatial gradient
and $a=\Phi_{xx}$ for its spatial derivative. Let $B$ be standard
Brownian motion and define the diffusion $X$ and its self-consistency function $q$ by
$$
dX_t=\gamma(t)u(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t,\qquad X_0=0,
\qquad q(t)=\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2].
$$
The discrepancy $q(t)-t$ enters the first variation of $\mathcal P$;
minimality will force $q(t)=t$ on the support of $\mu_\gamma$.
The SDE has a unique strong solution. All
stochastic calculations below take place on compact time intervals
ending before one, unless an endpoint limit is justified explicitly.

## 3. How a candidate receives its value To rule out a candidate, we will look for an allowed change that lowers its value. Adding mass at one scale changes the cumulative coefficient at every later scale. We therefore need both a value for each candidate and a way to compute the cost of that change. The auxiliary optimisation below supplies the value; its response to the starting state will enter the first-variation formula in Section 5.1. ### 3.1 First evaluate the zero coefficient The variational problem assigns each $\gamma$ a value by a one-dimensional auxiliary optimisation. Its final reward at state $x$ is $|x|$: this is the best one-spin score $\max_{\sigma\in\{-1,1\}}x\sigma$. First take $\gamma=0$, when only noise changes the state. The imported control representation uses noise with variance rate $\xi''$ ([Auffinger–Chen, Theorem 2][auffinger-chen]). Our normalisation $\xi(t)=t^2/2$ gives rate one, so the noise is **Brownian motion** $B$: a continuous random path starting at zero. Its increments over disjoint time intervals are independent; over an interval of length $h$, an increment has the law of the centred Gaussian $\sqrt h Z$. Starting at time $t$ in state $x$, the remaining noise $B_1-B_t$ therefore has the law of $\sqrt{1-t}Z$. The expected final reward is $$ \Phi_0(t,x)=\mathbb E|x+\sqrt{1-t}Z| =\int_{\mathbb R}|x+\sqrt{1-t}z|\varphi(z)\,dz. $$ At $(t,x)=(0,0)$ this is the calculation already performed: $\Phi_0(0,0)=\sqrt{2/\pi}$. At $t=1$ no noise remains and the value is $|x|$. The function gives an expected payoff at a specified starting state; it is not a probability density. ### 3.2 Allowing a response to the noise For a general $\gamma$, a response can bias the future state, with a quadratic cost. Here the overlap scale $t$ plays the role of time; the path is auxiliary, not a motion of the spins. The noise is the Brownian motion introduced above. A **control** $\alpha_s\in[-1,1]$ chooses a response at each time using only noise already observed since the starting time. The whole deterministic schedule $\gamma$ is known, but future noise is not. A rule chosen in advance can still give different responses on different observed paths. To see why this matters, let a sign $W=\pm1$, each with probability $1/2$, be revealed after a single choice $v\in[-1,1]$. The expected score $|W+v|-v^2/2$ is $1-v^2/2$, maximised at $v=0$. A choice $v=W$ would score $3/2$, but uses information unavailable at the time of choice. The continuous control problem repeats decisions with this same restriction; the finite example only illustrates that restriction. For a starting position $x$, the value is $$ \Phi_\gamma(t,x)=\sup_\alpha\mathbb E\left[ \left|x+B_1-B_t+\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s\,ds\right| -\frac12\int_t^1\gamma(s)\alpha_s^2\,ds \right]. $$ Inside the absolute value, noise and the accumulated bias change the state before its final reward is paid. The second integral is the running control cost. The supremum chooses the best permitted rule; its formal information condition is progressive measurability. Expectation now averages over Brownian paths for a fixed $\gamma$, rather than over spin couplings. At $\gamma=0$ both control terms vanish, recovering Section 3.1. The **Parisi functional** subtracts an explicit correction from this optimised value: $$ \mathcal P(\gamma)=\Phi_\gamma(0,0) -\frac12\int_0^1t\gamma(t)\,dt. $$ The inner supremum chooses a response for fixed $\gamma$; the outer problem minimises $\mathcal P$ over $\gamma$. ## 4. The full-support theorem

**Source theorem ([OpenAI (2026a), Theorem 1.1][support-manuscript]).**
In the pure, zero-field model with $\xi(t)=t^2/2$, let $\gamma$ be an
admissible integrable minimiser of $\mathcal P$. Its Stieltjes measure
has full relative support on $[0,1)$, and $\gamma$ is strictly increasing.
For every associated diffusion and every $0\le t<1$,

$$
\mathbb E[u(t,X_t)^2]=t,\qquad
\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^2]=1.
$$

The theorem requires a minimiser,
not merely an admissible candidate. Zero field supplies $q(0)=0$;
$\xi''=1$ enters the curvature estimate. The statement does not cover
nonzero field or general mixed-spin covariance functions.

## 5. Why a flat interval cannot minimise

We now prove the theorem. The identities $q=t$ and $q'=1$ are
conclusions still to be established. We begin with the first-order cost
of an allowed change, obtain conditions at support points, and then
exclude every possible gap.

### 5.1 Allowed changes and their first-order cost

The **first variation** in a direction $\eta$ is the derivative at
zero of $\varepsilon\mapsto\mathcal P(\gamma+\varepsilon\eta)$.
At a minimum its right derivative is nonnegative whenever small
$\varepsilon\ge0$ leave the candidate admissible. It need not vanish:
the opposite change may violate nonnegativity or monotonicity.
Precisely, let $\eta\in L^1(0,1)$, meaning $\int_0^1|\eta(t)|\,dt<\infty$, and suppose
$\gamma+\varepsilon\eta$ stays admissible for every
$0\le\varepsilon\le\varepsilon_0$, for some $\varepsilon_0>0$.
The formula is

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\eta]
=\frac12\int_0^1\eta(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt.
$$

Here $q$ belongs to the unperturbed candidate $\gamma$.
The term $-t/2$ comes from the outer correction in $\mathcal P$;
$q(t)/2$ is the sensitivity of the reoptimised control value. The latter
is the analytic content of the formula, not differentiation with a fixed
control. [Chen–Handschy–Lerman (2018), Proposition 4][chl-optimality]
gives the derivative along the segment joining any two admissible
coefficients. Taking the second endpoint to be
$\gamma+\varepsilon_0\eta$ and rescaling the segment parameter gives
the formula above. The detailed proof in
[OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 6.1][support-variation] compares value functions
and bounds the terminal remainder by the $L^1$ tail of $\eta$.

Adding a small atom at scale $s$ raises the cumulative function at
*every* later scale. It is always allowed: the total mass is not
fixed, so no compensating removal is required. Its direction is
$\eta(t)=\mathbf1_{[s,1)}(t)$, equal to zero before $s$ and one
from $s$ onward. Thus

$$
D\mathcal P(\gamma)[\mathbf1_{[s,1)}]
=\frac12\int_s^1(q(t)-t)\,dt=:\frac12G(s).
$$

For the candidate in Figure 1, adding $\varepsilon$ mass at $s=1/2$
creates a jump of height $\varepsilon$ there and raises the entire
remaining curve by $\varepsilon$. The coefficient changes only on
that tail, but its optimised value and feedback must be recomputed:
earlier starting states also face a changed future control problem. The
first-variation theorem accounts for this dependence. Its formula
has a tail integral because that is where the coefficient changes:
$G(s)/2$ is the marginal cost of placing mass at $s$. At a minimiser,
$G(s)\ge0$ for every $s<1$.

For the two weights in Section 2, the same accounting gives

$$
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
=2G(1/4)+G(3/4).
$$

Each weight is charged for its entire remaining tail. The $q$ and $G$
in this identity belong to that candidate; no optimality has been assumed.
Reducing both weights by a fraction $\varepsilon$ multiplies the
cumulative function by $1-\varepsilon$.

Suppose temporarily that this two-weight candidate minimised
$\mathcal P$. Addition would give two nonnegative costs,
$G(1/4)\ge0$ and $G(3/4)\ge0$, while the allowed reduction would give

$$
0\le-\frac12\bigl(2G(1/4)+G(3/4)\bigr).
$$

Both costs must be zero: their positive-weighted sum is nonnegative,
and the reduction forces it to be nonpositive. This is a necessary
condition under the temporary minimiser assumption, not a claim that
the two-weight candidate attains the minimum.

Now fix a general minimiser $\gamma$ and its own $q$, $G$ and
$\mu_\gamma$. The same argument replaces the finite sum by an integral.
The direction $\eta=-\gamma$
is integrable, and $(1-\varepsilon)\gamma$ remains admissible for
$0\le\varepsilon\le1$. It scales all existing mass by the same
factor. For the continuous candidate in Figure 1, it multiplies the
two nonzero slopes and the plateau height by $1-\varepsilon$;
it works for diffuse mass as well as atoms. To see the order of
integration, each weight at $s$ contributes for exactly the times
$t\ge s$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\int_0^1\gamma(t)(q(t)-t)\,dt
&=\int_0^1\int_{[0,1)}\mathbf1_{\{s\le t\}}(q(t)-t)\,\mu_\gamma(ds)\,dt\\
&=\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
\end{aligned}
$$

Thus the allowed reduction gives

$$
0\le D\mathcal P(\gamma)[-\gamma]
=-\frac12\int_{[0,1)}G(s)\,\mu_\gamma(ds).
$$

The exchange of integration order is valid even if the total mass is
infinite. Its absolute integral is bounded by the area from Section 2:

$$
\int_{[0,1)}\int_s^1|q(t)-t|\,dt\,\mu_\gamma(ds)
=\int_0^1\gamma(t)|q(t)-t|\,dt
\le\int_0^1\gamma(t)\,dt<\infty.
$$

Since $G\ge0$, its integral must be zero. If $G$ were positive at a
support point, continuity would bound it below by a positive number
on a neighbourhood carrying positive mass, contradicting that zero
integral. Hence $G=0$ on the support. This is **contact**: the
nonnegative function touches zero there. The scaling argument is the
variational argument of [Chen, Proposition 3.2, equations (3.11)–(3.12)][chen-support],
applied with the integrable-direction formula above.

Scaling removes only mass that exists. In Figure 1, even the supported

downward jump. For $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ the cumulative values would
remain nonnegative, but the function would no longer be nondecreasing.
Support alone does not permit atom removal. We have proved contact
on the support, not that every zero of $G$ must carry mass.

### 5.2 Contact gives endpoint conditions

We need information about $q$ at the ends of a possible gap. An interior
support point $s$ is a minimum of $G$. Since
$G'(s)=s-q(s)$ and $G''(s)=1-q'(s)$, ordinary calculus gives

$$
q(s)=s,\qquad q'(s)\le1.
$$

At zero, if it belongs to the support, contact and symmetry give
$G(0)=q(0)=0$. If $q'(0)>1$, continuity would give $q'(t)>1$
for small positive $t$. Integration would then give $q(t)>t$, so
$G'(t)=t-q(t)<0$. Starting from $G(0)=0$, this would force $G(t)<0$,
a contradiction. Hence $q'(0)\le1$. This one-sided argument includes
an atom at zero.

### 5.3 Strict curvature creates an impossible integral

The support is relatively closed in $[0,1)$. Starting at a missing
point, enlarge its mass-free interval until it reaches support or a
boundary of the domain. Such a maximal interval has two
support endpoints, starts at zero outside the support, or reaches one.
We treat these three cases in order; the last includes empty support.

First suppose $(r,s)$ has both endpoints in the support, with
$0\le r<s<1$. Its constant height $c$ is necessarily positive:
for $t$ inside the gap, a small relative neighbourhood of $r$ lies in

If $r=0$, this mass is an atom at zero. Contact imposes

$$
q(r)=r,\quad q(s)=s,\quad q'(r)\le1,\quad q'(s)\le1.
$$

The first two conditions require area $s-r$ under $q'$ across the gap.
A calculus model shows how strict convexity can prevent this. On the

$$

=\frac13\int_0^1[1-x(1-x)]\,dx=\frac5{18}.
$$

The missing area is $1/3-5/18=1/18$. This is a calculus model, not a
computed SK moment curve. The next input forces the actual $q'$ below

**Strict-curvature input ([OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][support-curvature]).**

$$
q'''(t)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]>0

Section 7.3 explains how this sign is obtained after expectation.
The gap argument uses its strict sign; it does not use the particular

The final inequality uses $a(t,x)>0$, proved by Gaussian smoothing

Because $q'''=(q')''$, the function $q'$ is strictly convex: between

The moment identity makes $q'$ continuous at the endpoints, even if

$$
q'(t)<\frac{s-t}{s-r}q'(r)+\frac{t-r}{s-r}q'(s)\le1
\qquad(r<t<s).
$$

### 7.2 The value equation and the moment identity

At $t=1$ there is no noise or response left to accumulate, so the value

Its partial differential equation (PDE) runs backward from that final value:

$$
\partial_t\Phi_\gamma
=-\frac12\left(\partial_{xx}\Phi_\gamma
+\gamma(t)(\partial_x\Phi_\gamma)^2\right),
\qquad \Phi_\gamma(1,x)=|x|.
$$

With the spatial derivatives $u$ and $a$ defined in Section 3.3,
the equation expresses
a recursive choice: choose a response for a short first step, then
use the best continuation from the state reached. At a continuity
point of $\gamma$, this gives the formal first-order relation

$$
\Phi_\gamma(t,x)
=\sup_{|v|\le1}\left\{
\mathbb E\Phi_\gamma(t+h,x+\gamma(t)vh+\sqrt hZ)
-\tfrac12\gamma(t)v^2h\right\}+o(h).
$$

Subtract the present value, divide by $h$, and Taylor-expand.
The identities $\mathbb EZ=0$ and $\mathbb EZ^2=1$ give

$$
0=\Phi_t+\tfrac12\Phi_{xx}

$$

The square completion from Section 3.3 gives a supremum of
$\gamma u^2/2$, attained at $v=u$, and hence the stated PDE. This calculation explains the equation;
justifying the recursion and the Taylor expansion requires the
control representation and regularity results. See

For each fixed $T<1$, the required spatial derivatives are bounded on
$[0,T]\times\mathbb R$, and step-coefficient and smooth-terminal
approximations justify the identities. The bounds depend on the coefficient
and strip. The PDE holds almost everywhere in time. These are not
bounds up to time one.

### 7.3 Where the strict-curvature input comes from

The proof in Section 5 used strict curvature on a positive constant
interval. We now explain how a correction with expectation zero makes
the estimate usable once the required density bounds and algebraic
identity are supplied. The sources construct the correction and prove
those bounds. Take any admissible
coefficient with $\gamma=c>0$ on an open interval, without assuming
minimality. Set $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$ there.
Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's rule gives

$$
q''=\mathbb E[b^2-2ca^3],\qquad
q'''=\mathbb E[d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4].
$$

The negative middle term prevents a pointwise positivity argument.
The source instead averages with the spatial probability density
$f_t(x)$ of $X_t$ at positive time. As in the half-time example,
for any integrable function $F$, grouping paths by their reached position gives

$$
\mathbb E[F(X_t)]=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x)f_t(x)\,dx.
$$

These are probability weights on states $x$, distinct from the
Stieltjes weights $\mu_\gamma(ds)$ on overlap scales. The proof needs
bounds relating this density to the spatial derivatives of the value.
The factorisation and comparison arguments establishing those bounds
are given in [OpenAI (2026a), §3][support-signs].

The operation can be written directly for the positive density $f_t$;

For a smooth function $F$ with integrable terms and vanishing boundary

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[F'(X_t)+F(X_t)\frac{f_t'(X_t)}{f_t(X_t)}\right]
=\int_{\mathbb R}(Ff_t)'(x)\,dx=0.

The source first uses positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficients with terminal approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh(Mx))$, choosing $M$ at least as large as every step height. The source's sign comparisons use this bound as well as smoothness. At this stage, write $R_c=d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4$. The source constructs a correction $C$ from the spatial derivatives and density, with $$ \mathbb E[C(t,X_t)]=0,\qquad R_c(t,x)+C(t,x)\ge\frac{c^2}{1000}a(t,x)^4. $$ A rational polynomial identity gives the second inequality by writing the remainder as a sum of nonnegative terms. The density bounds and vanishing boundary products justify the first. Consequently $$ q'''(t)=\mathbb E[R_c(t,X_t)] =\mathbb E[(R_c+C)(t,X_t)] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ This is how the correction produces a useful lower bound for the expectation even though $R_c$ can be negative at particular states. To reach an arbitrary admissible coefficient, fix a time inside the plateau and approximate in $L^1$ by step coefficients, keeping the same value $c$ near that time.
